David Ha, CEO of Sakana AI Intelligence emerges from constraints The T-shirt I’m wearing today has a diagram of world models on it. It was drawn by Professor Jürgen Schmidhuber himself back in 1990. Back then, compute was a million to a billion times more expensive than today, and he had to hand-draw these figures and paste them into the paper. Today we have AI scientists writing papers together with us, but it’s good to be reminded of how the innovations of the 1980s and 1990s led to where we are now. One of my hot takes on social media is that foundation models are among the fastest-depreciating financial assets in the history of mankind. As someone who started an AI company that makes these models, this is a real struggle for me. How does Japan compete with the rest of the world in this space? One of my core beliefs is that AI development is not just about throwing more compute and data into ever-larger models. I believe intelligence emerges from constraints. Modern AI scales through abundance, but biological intelligence emerged from scarcity. Evolution selects for doing more with less. Our brains, our language, and our culture are all proof that constraints drive intelligence. More than ten years ago, I got addicted to studying AI and took on some of the hardest tasks in OpenAI Gym. When I trained a neural network to solve the bipedal walker task, I also constrained the size of the robot and the energy it could use. With these constraints, the AI came up with a small, insect-like walker. What happens when there are no constraints at all? The AI discovered a giant robot with no brain that simply falls over toward the exit. We need constraints for our AI to actually have a brain. Discovering Professor Schmidhuber’s papers For the car racing task, where the agent drives from pixels, I gave the agent a world model, so that it could predict what would happen in the future and represent the world in a latent space. As Jürgen always tells us, I went back to look at what people had done in the past. That’s how I discovered his line of papers on world models, from his 1990 paper on making the world differentiable to his 2015 paper “On Learning to Think.” I found them very inspiring. They bring together many concepts, from algorithmic information theory to artificial curiosity, and that’s where I learned to think of an agent as a controller, C, and a model, M. I then wrote the “World Models” paper together with him, which we presented at NeurIPS. We showed that an agent can actually be trained inside the dream hallucinated by its own world model. These ideas now underpin many modern innovations, from self-driving cars to robotics. Sakana AI’s research and AI sovereignty in Japan In 2023, I co-founded Sakana AI with Llion Jones and Ren Ito. Sakana means fish in Japanese. We believe intelligence is not just about the individual fish; it’s the school, and we take a collective intelligence approach. As a company in Japan with limited resources, we also don’t want to do exactly what everyone else is doing. We want to be the red fish that swims a little differently from the rest. David Ha: "Intelligence is not just an individual fish. It's the school." Our research so far includes the brain-inspired Continuous Thought Machines , PC-ALM , which trains 1,000-layer networks without backpropagation, The AI Scientist, published in Nature this year , and the Darwin Gödel Machine , which brings Jürgen’s idea of the Gödel machine to life with LLMs. So how should Japan build AI amid global competition? I see AI sovereignty in Japan as resting on three pillars. Pre-training: the ability to develop this technology from scratch. Post-training: aligning models with our values, especially the values of Japan. And orchestration: combining our models with the frontier models produced by the rest of the world to push performance further. For orchestration we offer Sakana Fugu , and for post-training, Sakana Namazu . The last pillar is pre-training. We will be starting to pre-train our own models, and our Chief Scientist Takuya Akiba will talk about these efforts later today. Our plan is to pre-train an agent-native LLM and an agent-native world model, have them work together on difficult tasks, and improve them through a self-improvement loop driven by the AI Scientist. This plan doesn’t look that different from one of Professor Schmidhuber’s papers: a controller and a world model working together. With the tools available today, we can build on these great ideas from the past and push the frontier. Keynote | Jürgen Schmidhuber Next, Professor Jürgen Schmidhuber delivered the keynote. Neural networks were invented 230 years ago I’m really proud that David chose to show up in a T-shirt based on a drawing I made back in 1990. Modern AI is based on artificial neural networks. Your brain has about 100 billion neurons, each with maybe 10,000 connections on average. At first the strengths of these connections are random, but through learning some get stronger and some get weaker. That’s how the whole system learns to drive cars, translate languages, and do all kinds of things. Who invented artificial neural networks? Some people think it was someone in America, maybe around 1940, but that’s totally wrong. They were invented 230 years ago, between 1795 and 1805. In 1795, Gauss had exactly what was called a 2-layer linear neural network in the 1990s: weights on the connections between input and output units, adjusted so that the mean squared error on the training set is minimized. Back then it was called the method of least squares. The first to publish it was Legendre, in 1805. This Gauss–Legendre network is the core of what everybody is doing at all the famous companies today. The main difference is that today’s networks are deeper. By the way, the young Gauss became famous in 1801 by predicting the position of the asteroid Ceres after it had disappeared behind the sun. He predicted the next token, so to speak, and he got it right. The roots of deep learning, and Japan Who invented deep learning? It started in 1965 in Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union, with Ivakhnenko and Lapa. Ivakhnenko’s 1971 paper described an eight-layer network that learned to model the British economy by predicting the next value of a time series. Then, in 1967, a Japanese researcher, Shun-ichi Amari, introduced end-to-end deep learning, with a five-layer network, at a time when compute was billions of times more expensive than today. In 1970, Seppo Linnainmaa in Finland published what is now called backpropagation, used by everyone from Google to Sakana AI. Another great Japanese contribution came in 1979, when Kunihiko Fukushima introduced the first convolutional neural network, which he called the Neocognitron. There is a famous video from 1986 of it recognizing handwritten digits. In 1988, Wei Zhang, working at a lab in Japan, combined Fukushima’s convolutional network with backpropagation, and applied it to character recognition. Zhang also scaled it up in the 1990s. So convolutional neural networks, central to computer vision today, were invented and further developed and scaled in Japan. Since I’m here in Japan, I wanted to point out the essential things that happened in this country in the development of modern AI. Jürgen tracing the roots of modern AI, from Gauss to Fukushima World models and artificial curiosity, 1990 Our own contributions to neural nets came later, starting with this picture from 1990. There’s a little robot and a control network. One of the inputs is labeled R, for reward. The robot has pain sensors, and it receives evaluations of what it is doing as input. This is one essential ingredient of what is now called recursive self-improvement: a system that learns not only to do something, but also learns to improve the way it learns, and to improve the way it improves the way it learns, and so on, recursively. For that, the network must see the evaluations coming from the environment. That was already present back then. Then you add a second network, which looks at the robot’s actions and inputs and tries to predict what will happen next. That’s a model of the world. With a good model, you can plan: you can run mental experiments and choose the action sequences that lead to a lot of predicted reward and little pain. But in the beginning, the model knows nothing. That’s why you immediately need something like an artificial scientist, one that invents its own experiments. A baby does not learn by downloading the World Wide Web. If a baby moves its hand, the incoming video changes, and it learns to predict how. That’s how it learns about physics, how apples fall to the ground, how parents react when it cries. It creates its own data through self-invented experiments. The simplest way of doing this, which I published in 1990, is to have the world model minimize its error while the generative controller tries to maximize the same error. Whenever the controller finds a corner of the environment where the model can still learn something, it gets a reward: the eureka reward for inventing an experiment that tells you something you didn’t know. Many have implemented variants of this, and today this is called a generative adversarial network. I called it artificial curiosity. 1991, the miraculous year Back then, deep learning didn’t really work well. You couldn’t deal with long time lags, where something that happened a thousand steps ago influences something a thousand steps later. So in 1991 we had a whole bunch of papers to solve that problem, and funny enough, they are now the P and the T in ChatGPT. Pre-training: compressing long sequences by predicting the next thing. In the same paper, distilling the knowledge of one neural network into another. And the first Transformer variant. I called it the fast weight controller, but it is exactly what was called the linear Transformer in 2020. It scales linearly. With today’s quadratically scaling Transformer, if you have 1,000 times more text, you need a million times more compute. That is one of the reasons why data centers are so expensive. Also in 1991, my brilliant student Sepp Hochreiter introduced the principle of deep residual learning in his diploma thesis. Consider a very simple unit with a linear activation function and a connection to itself of weight 1.0. When you propagate errors back through time, you always multiply by 1.0, so nothing changes over thousands of steps. That is what enables very deep learning through gradient descent, and it’s the core of the LSTM. Later this led to the first deep residual feedforward network which we published under the name “Highway Network” in May 2015 (and then later “ResNet”). In 1991, nobody was interested in all of this. I once gave a talk at a conference where there was only one person in the audience, a young lady. I said, “Young lady, it’s very embarrassing, but apparently today I’m going to give this talk just to you.” She said, “Okay, but please hurry, I am the next speaker.” But every five years, computers got 10 times cheaper. Today compute is 10 million times cheaper than back then, and that’s why the techniques we published back then are now on all your smartphones. Planning without simulating every detail What David showed in his slide refers to a better way of planning. The naive way is to use the world model to simulate the future millisecond by millisecond. That’s good enough for chess and board games, but it’s not what you should do. When you plan a trip from here to Paris, you don’t simulate your hand grabbing the phone. You think of a few high-level things: call a taxi, go to the airport, check in. You make a compact plan and ignore the details. What I proposed in 2015 is to let the controller send queries into the hidden units of the world model, M. M may have seen all YouTube videos, or have lots of experience with robots. The controller is a learning prompt engineer that learns to address the few internal representations relevant to the current problem, interpret the answers, and change its own behavior. These queries are not in English or Japanese; they are just sequences of number vectors. For simple problems, it’s easier to solve them from scratch, but all interesting, complicated problems will greatly profit from the algorithmic information sitting deep in this huge model. In 2018, I also wrote a paper that collapses the model and the controller into one network through distillation. But the more famous paper of 2018 is the one by David, which showed in great experiments how world models can be really useful in practice. AI beyond the screen Let me put all this into a broader historical context. Much of what I mentioned today happened in Germany and Japan. In 1990, Japan seemed like the land of the future. The six most valuable companies in the world were all Japanese. In 1995, the nominal GDP of Japan and Germany together almost equaled that of America plus China. And in 2002, more than half of the world’s robots were from Japan, and the country with the second most robots was Germany. At the moment, the only AI that works really well is AI behind the screen. Behind the screen, there is a superhuman chess player, a superhuman Go player, a superhuman mathematician. But no robot comes close to what a plumber or an electrician can do, or to what a little boy can do with a football. Physical AI in the real world is not owned by anybody yet. We now see an opening for a robot that can learn, by demonstration and reinforcement, to operate all the existing tools and machines. Once we have that, machines can make more of themselves, and we have an ultimate scaling machine. Then it no longer matters how many people a country has; what matters is whether it has machines like that. I hope that Japan and Germany and maybe a few other robot-oriented countries will lead there, and maybe connect to former glory in this way. Jürgen on the promise of Physical AI The future is bright All the existing trends are working for the little guy, not for the big companies. Forty years ago, I knew a rich guy who had a mobile phone in his Porsche, so he could talk by satellite to another guy with a similar Porsche. Super expensive. Today, everybody all over the world has a smartphone that is much, much better. It’s going to be the same with AI. Every five years it gets 10 times cheaper, and the physical limits of this trend are still far away. Everybody is going to have lots of AIs making their lives longer, happier, and healthier. The future is bright. LLM Development at the RSI Lab | Takuya Akiba After a break, three researchers from Sakana AI’s RSI Lab gave talks. The RSI Lab has three teams: language models (LLM), world models, and recursive self-improvement (RSI). First up was Chief Scientist Takuya Akiba, who leads the LLM team. Chief Scientist, Takuya Akiba From the agent layer to the model layer Sakana AI was founded in 2023, and I joined as one of its earliest members. I’ve worked on a variety of things, and one of our focuses has been the agent layer: assuming strong models exist, and researching how to use them to do interesting things. One example is ALE-Agent , an agent designed to discover strong algorithms for combinatorial optimization. We entered it in live competitive programming contests, and after a few attempts, it took first place against human experts . Another is AB-MCTS , a general algorithm for inference-time scaling that calls language models repeatedly to solve very hard problems. It has been deployed in multiple real-world projects at Sakana AI. Working at the agent layer has been fun and successful. But recently, I think the model layer has become attractive again. Recent open models are very strong, close to frontier models, and good enough for real work. Data, training recipes, and software have become more accessible, so building these models is getting cheaper. Perhaps more importantly, specialization at the model layer has become a very attractive option. With agentic reinforcement learning, we can optimize models end-to-end for our own tools, workloads, and scaffolds, and sometimes these specialized models outperform general ones. This year we released Sakana Namazu , a model based on an open model and post-trained mainly for Japanese users. We reduced geopolitical bias, improved its understanding of Japanese culture, and taught it ways of communicating and thinking that feel more natural to Japanese users. Then, this summer, we launched the RSI Lab, with three teams: language models, world models, and RSI research. I represent the language model team. Sakana Sawara So what’s next at the RSI Lab? Today I’d like to introduce our new language model series, Sakana Sawara. Please note that this is still a provisional name. Takuya Akiba introducing the new language model series "Sakana Sawara" (provisional name) Sawara will be our own language model series, built entirely by us from scratch. With Namazu we focused on post-training existing open models; with Sawara we are expanding into pre-training. It won’t be adapted from any other model, so we have full control over it. And it will be an agent-native language model, designed from the start for agentic workloads such as tool-integrated reasoning, coding, and long-horizon tasks. Sawara will serve two purposes. One is to be the foundation of Sakana AI’s products and solutions. The other is to be the foundation of our RSI research. Because we have full control over the model and the recipes, and every process is fully transparent to us, it will enable RSI research with a broader scope. Unfortunately, I don’t have much to share about Sawara yet, because it is still under development. So today I’d like to talk about how I think about language model development: my strategy. The four features of Sawara LLM development is a research competition Many people would agree that this competition is about using more and more GPUs. That’s 100% true. But many also think GPUs are mainly for scaling, that is, for increasing the number of parameters or pre-training tokens. That is actually a misunderstanding. According to Epoch AI , many groups use only a fraction of their compute for final training runs. At OpenAI, for example, final training runs are estimated to have accounted for only about 10% of R&D compute. A large share goes into trial and error, in other words, research. Language model development is more of a research competition than you might imagine. So what are the key factors in this competition? I’d say progress is the product of two things: compute and research efficiency. Compute is simple. More GPUs means more experiments. Research efficiency is underestimated, but it’s equally important, because the result is the product of the two. It’s about how much we can learn from each experiment. Over the past ten years, I’ve seen a huge difference here between researchers. Some people are very good at designing experiments that give us as much information as possible. Talent density and AI tokens at scale What drives a team’s research capability today? I’d say talent density and AI tokens at scale. It’s 2026, not 2023. Since we published the AI Scientist in 2024, many groups have followed, and everyone now agrees that research is a collaboration between humans and AI. We emphasize talent density over headcount, and I’m confident in my team. It’s the most talent-dense team I have ever seen. Interestingly, this way of thinking leads continuously to RSI. We are already using AI, but it’s probably not our own models. Next time, some part of that AI could be Sawara. Then the next version of Sawara could be developed with the help of Sawara. It depends on how you define RSI, but I’d call this fractional RSI. Hopefully, in the future, Sawara will take on more and more of this process. Roadmap Finally, our roadmap. We are now preparing for training, and we will start pre-training Sawara Small (provisional name) this December. If everything goes smoothly, we will release the weights next spring. We also plan to develop a larger model, Sawara Large (provisional name). Towards Open-Ended Autonomous Discovery Systems | Robert Tjarko Lange Next, Staff Research Scientist Robert Tjarko Lange spoke on behalf of the RSI team. Robert Tjarko Lange on Open-Ended Autonomous Discovery Systems The AI Scientist so far When I started my scientific career, one of my big inspirations was Jürgen’s diploma thesis, on genetic algorithms that recursively refine themselves. That’s how I started working on meta-learning. Today, in 2026, we have much more powerful mutation operators in the form of large language models, which let us autonomously test new hypotheses. Scientific progress drives prosperity, but so far most research has been done purely by humans, without AI assistance. So in 2024, as language models began to follow instructions well, we started building the AI Scientist v1 , a blueprint for automating the entire research pipeline with agents, from ideation and novelty checks to experiments, paper writing, and review. A year later, with v2, we used tree search to orchestrate the stages of the research pipeline, and a paper it generated passed human peer review at a machine learning conference workshop . We obtained ethics approval in advance and communicated closely with the workshop organizers, because we always want to respect the scientific process and maintain integrity. Our latest version, v3, also called the Agentic Scientist, can still run fully autonomously, but it is designed for co-discovery, so that humans can work with it to refine hypotheses. It verifies all claims, runs ablations, and aims to reduce reward hacking. We used v3 to write another paper, which we submitted after checking all the claims ourselves, and it was accepted as a main conference paper at ALIFE 2026. Robert on the milestones of the AI Scientist Broadening the ideation radius So what’s next? Many auto-research systems today are a bit like hyperparameter tuning on steroids. They can rewrite code, but their ideation radius is not how humans do research. We need to move beyond hill-climbing benchmarks and push these systems to do research in a much more diverse way. For inspiration, we can look at Sakana AI’s own structure: the Frontier Intelligence Group (FIG) , where researchers explore interesting, long-horizon hypotheses in an open-ended way. How can we build AI scientists in that spirit, less hill-climbed? Human scientists are biologists, economists, and philosophers. To advance science holistically, we need AI scientists that adapt to different disciplines, gather their own expertise, and improve themselves. Additionally, 80% of my own scientific process is trial and error that never makes it into the final paper. These scientific research traces are largely absent from the LLM training process. We need to explicitly think about how AI systems can internalize the scientific method itself, drawing on ideas like Karl Popper’s falsificationism. Science is inherently a collective endeavor, not a lone genius in a corner. How do we build a world where AI scientists collaborate collectively, and where humans are part of that process too? The technical questions become how to allocate resources, how to assign credit to scientific results, and how to judge whether a contribution is meaningful. Finally, safety is really important. But I think the solution is not to stop AI progress, but to use AI to develop AI safely. Applying AI scientists to areas like mechanistic interpretability or chain-of-thought monitoring can give us not only better systems, but also a better understanding of them. World Models & Physical AI | Stefania Druga / Sebastian Risi The third talk, on world models and Physical AI, was given by Stefania Druga and Sebastian Risi. Why Physical AI in Japan (Stefania) We are very excited to do this work in Japan, because Japan excels at robotics and Physical AI. At the same time, Japan faces big challenges: three out of ten people are over 65. That is both a problem and an opportunity. If we combine the hardware capabilities here with what AI can learn today, we can create better applications for the people who need them most. Sebastian Risi (left) and Stefania Druga (right) Check with a world model before acting in the real world (Sebastian) Robot learning has made great progress over the past ten years. But we still don’t see robots in our households, and as Jürgen said, we don’t have robot plumbers or electricians yet. I think two gaps remain: speed and safety. Approaches that use big LLMs are slow at inference. And even when tasks succeed, 18 to 28% of episodes don’t follow the instructions exactly. Our bet at Sakana for closing these gaps is world models. You check actions with a world model before performing them in the real world, and you only accept improvements backed by actual physical evidence. Physical trials are very costly, so robots need a world model that lets them imagine potential futures. In our architecture, a small vision-language model (VLM), which allows fast inference, proposes plans. The world model takes these plans, predicts states several steps ahead, judges feasibility and causes of failure, and scores how close the plan gets to the goal. Many plans are filtered out by the world model, only a few are tried on real hardware, and the results are used to improve the VLM. Sebastian explaining the improvement loop that combines world models and real hardware But what we want is recursive self-improvement: a system that not only gets better, but gets better at getting better. We connect the Agentic Scientist, the agent-native LLM we are developing, and Physical AI, so that the Agentic Scientist can improve the world model itself, and we feed what we learn from the real world back into the Agentic Scientist to close the loop. To avoid reward hacking, we use a frozen gate with strict criteria: repeated gains across evaluations, statistical evidence, and gains on held-out tasks. And building on collective intelligence, which is in Sakana’s DNA, we are also working on making RSI more effective and safer . Stefania presenting early experiments in world models and Physical AI Early experiments (Stefania) A world model predicts what’s next, but an experiment tells us what actually happens. We want to close the gap between the two and learn recursively. In our first example, in partnership with AIRoA (AI Robot Association), we took a fine-tuned π0.5 policy and tested it in simulation on a Franka robot. At first, the robot couldn’t open a drawer or place objects in it. By repeatedly showing the controller where it failed, we improved it until the robot succeeded. The next step is to test the improved policy in the real world. We have also started working on robots that change their own morphology depending on the task. We create simulations from real robot videos, explore in simulation, which is faster, cheaper, and safer, test the resulting controller on the physical robot, and feed the results back. In a simple example, we went through this entire loop. This doesn’t stop at robotics. I connected a microscope and a set of sensors to Sakana’s Agentic Scientist (v3) to forecast the best lighting conditions for collecting data, and then let the system change the lighting itself. Better experiments lead to better models, and better models lead to better experiments. The world is changing. We are modeling the world, machines are adapting to the world we are modeling, and people are changing as well. We want to design a world where people and machines co-evolve in safe and flourishing ways. Fireside Chat | David Ha × Jürgen Schmidhuber The final session was a conversation between David Ha and Jürgen, moderated by Stefania Druga. David Ha and Jürgen in conversation, moderated by Stefania Druga It started with an email Stefania: How did your “World Models” paper come about? David: I was at the NeurIPS 2016 Deep RL workshop, where Jürgen was giving a talk on his paper “On Learning to Think.” That inspired me to learn more about world models. Then I tried to win OpenAI’s car racing task and implemented one of the world model variants. I sent Jürgen my preliminary results, we agreed to turn it into a proper paper with additional experiments, and we presented it at NeurIPS as an oral presentation. Jürgen: You really have to emphasize that this was all driven by David. And it was not just an oral; it was among the top 2% or so of accepted papers. Stefania: What did you think when you received that email with the car animation? Jürgen: It was one of the most charming emails I’ve ever gotten. Eight years on Stefania: It has been eight years since the paper. How has research on world models evolved, and what surprised you? David: We’re seeing tremendous progress in scaling up world models; they’re now used in self-driving cars. But I’m surprised by the lack of novelty. Humans can arrive at a decision intuitively, with a controller working together with a predictor. Yet in robotics, everyone still seems to run Monte Carlo tree search simulations at every planning step. That’s where I hope our work at Sakana AI, leveraging AI scientists, can help advance world models, especially in Physical AI. Jürgen: The main lesson was: just be patient. Every five years, computers get 10 times cheaper. In a couple of decades we will have another factor of a million, and everything that seems impressive today will seem trivial in hindsight. On the other hand, physical robots don’t evolve as quickly as computers. Thirty years ago, there were pretty decent walking robots in Japan. Today’s robots are maybe three to five times better, not a million times better. Physical AI is a slow game. What it takes to be a researcher now Stefania: Agentic coding has shifted developers’ identity, and now we’re seeing the same with scientists. How should people deal with this change? David: The baseline keeps moving higher. If I applied for a job at any AI company today, including our own, I’d probably fail the interview. Three years ago, we looked for interns who could come up with ideas, implement experiments, and collect results. Now you can ask an AI agent to do that, so we expect interns to think like a professor or a PI. Scientists have to think like meta-scientists, and meta-scientists like meta-meta-scientists. It’s turtles all the way down. But there’s one thing I believe will stand the test of time, and I like to call it vision. An example I often bring up in Japan is Nintendo. Nintendo didn’t chase state-of-the-art performance. They stayed true to their vision of creating fun games, and they didn’t need the best hardware to succeed. As long as we have our own vision and mission, we can use technology to achieve it as the technology improves. Jürgen: It’s interesting to see which kinds of artificial scientists are working. The one that has improved dramatically is the artificial mathematician. Mathematics is deductive: the rules are given as axioms, and you can stay behind the screen and search for a proof or a disproof. Physics is very different. You don’t know the rules of the game. You have to take the raw pixels coming at you and distill a new physical law that wasn’t known before. That’s induction, and it’s much harder. I always claim that the first time an artificial physicist discovers a new physical law will be roughly the same time an artificial musician first creates a melody as good as one of the 100 best melodies in human history. David Ha and Jürgen during the fireside chat Closing Perhaps half of the AI Jürgen has envisioned has been realized through generative AI. The other half, such as artificial scientists that invent their own experiments to understand the world, and Physical AI that works in the real world, has yet to scale. AI research today may look dominated by US and Chinese players competing to scale ever-larger foundation models, but this opportunity is open, perhaps even more so, outside the big labs. Japan is one of the most promising places to pursue it. Sakana AI was founded to build a frontier AI company in Japan, bringing together researchers from around the world and top researchers from Japan. At the RSI Lab , launched in June 2026, we are pursuing next-generation language models starting with Sawara, AI-driven AI research, and, combined with these, research on world models and Physical AI, all at once. Jürgen will continue to provide insight and inspiration for this challenge. We hope this symposium will be one of the starting points for opening up the next era of AI, together with companies and research institutions across Japan. Thank you to everyone who joined us. Sakana AI Sakana AI is hiring across research, engineering, and business, including at the RSI Lab. Learn more about the RSI Lab: https://sakana.ai/rsi-lab/ Open positions: https://sakana.ai/careers/

abstract: Sakana AIは、金融と並ぶ注力領域として「防衛・インテリジェンス」に取り組んでいます。AIが人間には読み切れない量のデータから仮説をつくり、分析者がその仮説を根拠とともに使える状態を目指しています。 今年3月には読売新聞社と共同で、SNS上の110万件の投稿から中国による対日批判のナラティブを分析しました。 この分析では、AIが立てた仮説を記者の取材によって裏付けています。 SNSは一見、世論を映す鏡のように思えますが、投稿の数を数えるだけでは見落とすことが多くあります。たとえば選挙前に支持が厚く見えた候補が、実は党内の動員に支えられていただけだったり、急に増えた反応のほとんどが実は批判だったりします。本当の情勢をつかむには、数十万件の言葉を「誰が・なぜ書いたのか」まで遡って読む必要があります。 AIを使えば、こうした投稿の内容にまで踏み込んだSNS分析が可能になります。今回はそのケーススタディとして、11月3日に投票が行われる米国中間選挙を分析しました。 ▶ レポート全文（PDF）： 米中間選挙のAI分析 — テキサス州上院選 SNSからのナラティブ分析 Sakana AIのナラティブ分析システムは、言説を「誰が・何をして・それがどう評価されるか」という物語の単位で取り出し、その物語を自分の言葉で語り直した人の数で広がりを測ります。抽出した物語は複数のAIモデルが原文と照合し、確かめられたものだけをレポートに残しました。今回の約71万件の反応についても、支持・批判の比率を統計的な誤差幅つきで推定しています。 仮説の深層分析 SNSの中だけを見ていると、言説空間のゆがみに気づけないことがあります。そこで長時間の推論で深いリサーチを行う当社のプロダクト「 Sakana Marlin 」に世論調査、選挙資金、予測市場、報道などの公開情報を調べさせ、X上の観測と突き合わせました。Marlinは複数のAIが仮説を並行して探り、互いに評価し合う仕組みを持っています。Marlinを駆使することで、SNSの内と外のどちらで先に変化が起こったかを、出典つきで辿ることが可能になりました。 テキサス州上院選で分かったこと 約30年にわたって共和党が勝ち続けてきたテキサス州で、今回の上院選は接戦が予想されています。上記のようなAIを駆使して、両候補と両党の州組織によるXへの発信2,042件と、それに寄せられた反応70万5,976件を分析したところ、たとえば次のようなことが分かりました。 共和党の決選投票前にパクストン候補へ寄せられていた「支持」の多くは、党内の指名争いに向けた動員でした。決選が終わると、支持の割合は約5割から2割弱に下がりました。 両候補のリプライ欄で交わされていたのは、二つの陣営が互いに相手の欄へ出向いて攻撃し合う応酬でした。こうした反応の中身と推移を読み解くと、タラリコ候補の相対的な優勢は6月に示され、候補者の資質、経済、宗教、データセンターと主な争点が変化する中で、終盤で僅差の接戦となっていることが分かりました。 X上の言説は、パクストン候補への評価の転変や宗教やデータセンターをめぐる両候補のナラティブとその評価など、世論調査には現れない複雑な動きを示していました。また、両候補者への評価の転換は、Cook Political Reportなどの主要評価機関が判断を変える約2か月前に現れていました。 AIとの協働で行うインテリジェンスへ 上記のような知見は、人間とAIのどちらかだけでは導くことはできないものだと言えます。Sakana AIが先日発表した 「The AI Scientist」の最新版 では、人とAIがともに科学的発見を行う「Co-Discovery」を、これからの科学のあり方として提案しました。こうした人とAIの協働の重要性は、インテリジェンスの領域でも同じだと考えられます。AIは、人間には読み切れない規模の情報から仮説を導き、根拠とともに提示します。それを受け取った人間は仮説を吟味し、取材や追加の観測を行ったうえで判断を下します。AIを駆使して分析し、洞察を導き、最終的な判断は人間が担う。こうしたAIと人間の協働が、AI時代のインテリジェンスのあり方だと私たちは考えています。 テキサス州上院選の分析の詳細は、レポート全文にまとめています。 ▶ レポート全文（PDF）： 米中間選挙のAI分析 — テキサス州上院選 Sakana AI Sakana AIは、AIの未来を私たちと一緒に切り拓いてくださる方を募集しています。当社の 募集要項 をご覧ください。
title: Intelligence Report: SNSのAI分析からみる米中間選挙

abstract: 管理画面のイメージ。*この画像は架空のデータを使ったイメージです。今後予告なく変更される可能性があります。 管理画面のイメージ。*この画像は架空のデータを使ったイメージです。今後予告なく変更される可能性があります。 （English Announcement Below.） Sakana AIは本日、エンタープライズのお客様向けの Sakana API Platform を発表し、そのアーリーアクセスプログラムを開始しました。Sakana API Platformでは、Sakana AIが提供するLLMを、APIを通じて管理機能とともに利用できます。これにより、組織やワークスペース単位で利用料やメンバーを一元管理でき、エンタープライズのお客様でも安心して利用できるようになります。また、OpenAI互換のAPIを採用しており、すでにアプリに組み込まれているLLMのAPI呼び出し方式を変えず接続先を変えるだけですぐに利用できます。ご希望のお客様は、以下よりお申込み下さい。 👉 アーリーアクセスプログラムに申込む Sakana API Platformとは Sakana API Platformとは、エンタープライズのお客様向けにSakana AIのLLMおよび製品を、企業の運用に合わせて活用し、アプリケーションやシステムから呼び出すためのインターフェースです。モデルを呼び出すAPIに加えて、企業での運用に必要な管理機能を提供します。 Sakana FuguとSakana Namazuの各モデルは、これまで管理機能を伴わないAPIとして提供してきました。Sakana API Platformでは、これらのモデルを組織の管理のもとで利用できるようになります。利用権限や利用量を管理できるため、小規模なチームから大規模な組織まで、同じ仕組みでお使いいただけます。 APIを通じて提供するモデルは、まずはSakana Fugu、Sakana Fugu Ultraを提供し、Sakana NamazuおよびSakana Fugu Maxは順次提供予定です。 Sakana Fugu は、複数のフロンティアモデルを編成するオーケストレーション基盤モデルです。お客様のワークロードに最適なモデルの組み合わせを編成します。本技術は、ICLR 2026に採択された研究（Trinity、Conductor）に基づくものです。ラインナップは、Fugu（標準）と、Fugu Ultra、Fugu Maxの3つです。モデルの詳細は こちら をご覧ください。 Sakana Namazu は、日本語に特化したLLMです。日本の文脈に馴染んだ知能を、導入しやすい価格で提供します。モデルの詳細は こちら をご覧ください。 管理機能としては、組織の下にワークスペースを作り、チームや環境ごとの設定をしたり、チームの利用状況を把握できます。 主な機能一覧 組織・ワークスペース管理と管理コンソール（メンバー、APIキー、利用量を一元管理） ロールベースのアクセス制御 監査ログ（CSVダウンロード）、入力データを学習に使用しないことをデータ取扱条件として明示 予算上限設定、請求書払い対応、MSAおよびDPA、など 今後も、組織単位での詳細な権限制御など、機能を拡充する予定です。 アーリーアクセスプログラムについて お申し込みいただいたお客様のうち、当社側の準備が整ったお客様から順に、一般提供に先立ってご利用いただけます。お申し込み内容を確認のうえ、個別にご連絡いたします。料金およびご利用条件は、ご案内の際にお伝えします。 👉 アーリーアクセスプログラムに申込む Sakana AI Sakana AIでは、Sakana API Platformのようなプロダクトを、お客さまの現場に届けていく仲間を募集しています。当社の 募集要項 をご覧ください。 English Announcement Sakana API Platform: Early Access Program Now Open for Enterprises An illustration of the admin console. This image uses demo data and may change without notice. Today, Sakana AI announced the Sakana API Platform for enterprise customers and opened its Early Access program. With Sakana API Platform, you can use LLMs from Sakana AI through an API, together with management features. Organizations can manage usage costs and members in one place, by organization and workspace, so enterprises can adopt it with confidence. The API is OpenAI-compatible: if your applications already call an LLM API, you only need to change the endpoint. To apply, please use the link below. 👉 Apply for Early Access Program What is the Sakana API Platform? Sakana API Platform is the entry point for enterprise customers to use Sakana AI’s models and products in their own operations, calling them from applications and systems. It also provides the management features that enterprise operations require. Until now, the Fugu and Namazu models have been offered as standalone APIs. Sakana API Platform lets organizations of any size use them under more controlled management, with confidence. Sakana Fugu and Sakana Fugu Ultra are available first. Sakana Namazu and Sakana Fugu Max will follow. Sakana Fugu is an orchestration foundation model that orchestrates multiple frontier models. It assembles the combination of models best suited to your workload. It builds on research accepted at ICLR 2026 (Trinity and Conductor). The lineup has three models: Fugu (standard), Fugu Ultra, and Fugu Max. For details, see here . Sakana Namazu is an LLM specialized in Japanese. It offers intelligence attuned to the Japanese context. For details, see here . For management, you can create workspaces under your organization, configure settings for each team or environment, and see how each team is using the platform. Key features Organization and workspace management, with an admin console (members, API keys, and usage in one place) Role-based access control Audit logs (CSV download), and data handling terms that state your inputs are not used for training Budget limits, invoice payment, MSA and DPA, and more We plan to keep expanding these features, including more granular permission controls at the organization level. About Early Access Program We will offer access to applicants as they become ready, and contact each applicant individually after reviewing their application. Pricing and terms of use will be shared at that time. 👉 Apply for Early Access Program Sakana AI At Sakana AI, we are looking for teammates who will bring products like Sakana API Platform to our customers where they work. See our open positions .
title: Sakana API Platform、エンタープライズ向けにアーリーアクセスプログラムを開始

abstract: Switch to the Japanese section - 日本語版はこちら In 2026, Sakana AI released a series of products: Sakana Chat, Sakana Marlin, Sakana Fugu, and Sakana Translate. Known until now as an R&D company, Sakana AI has entered the stage of delivering products born from its research to companies and government agencies. The Go-To-Market (GTM) team that sells and scales those products launched in earnest in September 2026. Leading the team is Hidekazu Kakishima, who has driven the business launches of new technologies like cloud, IoT, and drones right from the dawn of their respective industries. Why Sakana AI, and why now? How do you sell products that come out of research, and what kind of team do you build to grow them? And what makes it interesting to join a team that still has few established systems? We sat down with him to find out. Interviewee Hidekazu Kakishima VP of GTM Led the strategic accounts team during the early days of AWS Japan, then joined IoT connectivity startup SORACOM as a founding member, and later drove the real-world adoption of flying robotics at US drone maker Skydio. He now leads market expansion and value delivery for Sakana AI’s product lineup. The Frontier of Technology Draws Talented People Who Love What’s New — From AWS to SORACOM, Skydio, and now Sakana AI, you seem to have chosen the early days of a new technology every time. Tell us about your career. At the root is a belief that technology makes the world better. That is why I have always wanted to work at the leading edge of fields where new technology is emerging. I was not that conscious of it in my twenties, but once I encountered cloud computing at AWS, I switched firmly into that mode. After that came IoT at SORACOM, drones at Skydio, and now AI. Each is a field where a new industry is being born, and my job is to take the technology at the frontier and put it to work in the market from the inside. That is what I want to do, and I have chosen every step of my career by that standard. There is one more reason I keep choosing the launch phase. When a new trend emerges, its leading edge attracts talented people who love new things. Learning the latest technology, implementing it, and seeing customers happy is enjoyable in itself. But working alongside those people is the particular pleasure of the early days. — Given that, why Sakana AI? Because I thought it was the best AI company in Japan. It is growing fast as a startup, its valuation is rising rapidly, and it is a Japan-born company aiming at the global market with research and development as its foundation. I had been following the company for some time. Then an acquaintance introduced me, and I had the chance to actually hear the story. Before joining, I spoke with Ren Ito, co-founder and chairman. Hearing his vision of scaling Sakana AI as a business not just in Japan but globally was exciting. The founders and the members are all wonderful people, and in the end, the desire to work with good people was what decided it. Because the company started from R&D, it has excellent technology and attracts talented people. But turning that into something the world can use is not easy. I felt the company was building a team for exactly that and expanding rapidly, and the GTM team now owns that part: making it usable. From Research Insights to Products That Reach More Customers — Let’s talk about that mission of making the technology usable. Where does the GTM team stand today? Alongside its research, Sakana AI has focused on industries such as finance and defense and implemented AI on the ground at customers. We have now entered a phase of turning the knowledge accumulated there into products and delivering them to a broader range of customers. That said, releasing a product does not mean customers can use it right away. There will always be situations where the product alone cannot meet a customer’s requirements. To close that gap, we are currently hiring Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs). FDEs feed what they learn at the customer’s site back into the product. As that accumulates, we want to increase the number of cases where the product can be used on its own, without an FDE. Many AI companies are investing in the FDE role right now. At the same time, people sometimes ask how it differs from an engineer who goes on site and builds things for the customer. The difference is precisely this feedback loop. Solving the customer’s problem is not the end. Reflecting that experience back into product improvement is part of the job. That is the role of an FDE at Sakana AI and the model we are aiming for. The Product Opens the Conversation; the Customer’s Problem Is What We Solve — The job descriptions for the GTM team use the phrase “product-driven GTM.” It sounds different from both system-integrator development and deploying a SaaS product as is. What is the approach? When people hear “product-driven,” many picture a one-way push to sell a product that already exists. Our stance is a little different. For us, product-driven means using the product as the starting point for a conversation with the customer. We present the product first, watch the customer’s reaction, and then propose the best way to apply it as a solution. It is less about going out to sell a product and more about matching the product to the customer’s problem. There are also cases where the customer does not know how to implement it, or where security has to be tailored to specific requirements. These requirements differ by industry and by company, so an FDE steps in to move the deployment forward. When there are no special requirements, customers can use the product as is. Our API services, for example, are called directly from the customer’s own systems. Sakana Marlin is a research product for business users, aimed mainly at people who do research work every day. — We understand you are not selling only through your own team, but also place importance on working with partners. Our resources are limited, so partners are essential. One type is system integrators, whom we are encouraging to build Sakana AI products into their own solutions. The other is technology companies with partner ecosystems, where Sakana AI products are offered through their marketplaces. This model lets us grow the user base not just in Japan but globally. Orchestrating Multiple Models, and the Growing Demand for AI Sovereignty — A bit more on products. Orchestration, which brings in multiple frontier models, is one of Sakana AI’s technical strengths. How are customers responding? Many companies have recently released features that let you switch between different models. Sakana Fugu does not simply switch models, though. It takes the approach of having multiple frontier models work together on a single task. I think that is a very distinctive feature. Behind the demand for this approach is a wariness about continuing to depend on a single model, however good it is. In February 2026, the US government instructed federal agencies to stop using Anthropic products, and the US Department of Defense designated the company a supply chain risk. No matter how strong the performance, a model can become unavailable for political or contractual reasons. Many companies must have felt that firsthand. More and more companies want to use multiple models, and this approach is drawing attention. We also hear concerns that a particular model could suddenly become unavailable. For better or worse, these circumstances are a tailwind, and we are receiving inquiries from many customers. — Are you seeing changes in customer attitudes around AI sovereignty as well? I think so. AI is a bigger trend than anything before it, and precisely because of that, awareness of security is extremely high. Awareness of AI sovereignty and data sovereignty is rising among both customers themselves and governments, and requests of this kind are clearly increasing. And it is not limited to large companies. Small and medium-sized businesses are also interested from a data sovereignty perspective. It has become a theme shared across a wide range of customers. — Demand is high, yet both customers and sellers still seem to be feeling their way. Compared with cloud and IoT, which you have worked on before, what is the same and what is different? First, the AI market is overwhelmingly larger. Beyond that, the customer’s situation is different. Cloud had an easy-to-understand framing as a replacement for on-premises. IoT had M2M communications before it, so customers understood it quickly, and the decision was often simply to migrate if it improved efficiency. AI is not like that. The customers themselves are feeling their way. They do not know what to do. And because information from around the world now arrives flat over the internet, AI players and customers are struggling at the same time. That makes the job of selling harder. Still, customers have a strong sense that they have to do something. We can approach them exactly where they do not know how, so the business is moving at tremendous speed. On the other hand, models are evolving so quickly that customers tend to avoid long-term commitments. They also want an environment they can use with confidence and safety. — In that market, where do you aim to be in one year and in three? The immediate priority is to build up effective deployment results with customers in Japan. But when it comes to expanding globally, waiting until we have a track record in Japan and then taking it overseas would be too slow. So we are moving with the intention of pursuing Japan and overseas in parallel from the start. In Japan, we will expand broadly through collaboration with the investors who have backed us and through partnerships with a range of partners. Overseas, the thinking is the same: build results with the overseas big tech companies and other investors who have backed us, and scale from there. Ideally, in three years, overseas will account for the larger share. We Want People Who Enjoy an Environment That Changes Fast — Let’s turn to the team. The GTM team is hiring for several roles: Account Executive, FDE, Partner Alliances, and Customer Success. For each role, what kind of person do you want to join? Let me start with what applies to every role. One is enjoying change. Both the industry and the company are moving very dramatically right now, and we want people who can enjoy that and thrive in it. The other is curiosity. Building your work while engaging with a wide range of people, including customers, the industry, and colleagues inside the company, requires curiosity. On top of that, for Account Executives, the market is large and we expect the deal sizes we sell to grow dynamically. We are looking for people who have built large businesses from zero and closed large deals. Partner Alliances handles the collaboration with system integrators and ecosystems I mentioned earlier. It is a job of designing from scratch who we partner with and how we sell together. — What kind of person are you looking for as an FDE? For FDEs, I do not want them to start from “we can’t” when a customer makes a request. The role is to look at the customer’s requirements against our capabilities from a technical standpoint and close the gap between them. Someone who can carry a problem through from discovery to resolution on the technical side is a good fit. Beyond that, we want people who can look broadly for the next problem and the next opportunity, even outside their scope. Do not stop at solving the issue. Find what is needed next and connect it to product improvement. That is an FDE at Sakana AI. — Customer Success, a new role you are hiring for, handles customers after deployment, correct? Yes, it handles follow-up after a customer has deployed. Because models evolve quickly, we need to keep checking whether customers are using them properly and whether new issues have emerged. We will be releasing products aggressively from here on, so combining them into a more efficient setup for the customer is also part of Customer Success’s job. By the nature of the role, Account Executives move on to the next customer. If deployed customers are left alone, they may switch to another company or simply lose track of what to do. Supporting them there is a very important role. Speaking at a Datadog event, October 2026 Now Is the Only Time You Can Build the System With Us — What can you gain by joining the GTM team now? There is still a great deal that has not been systematized, so you get to build those systems with us. That is the biggest thing. Members from a range of backgrounds are joining, each bringing their own ways of thinking and opinions to the discussion. That produces new insights, and moments where you realize what it means to build something new. Opportunities for this kind of experience are rare. Building from zero at a company riding the big wave of AI is a valuable experience. And then, from Japan to the world. This is a challenge only Sakana AI can offer. Sakana AI’s development base is in Tokyo. The researchers and the product development team sit at the desks right next to the GTM team. Feedback and feature requests from customers can be discussed with the development side on the spot and reflected in the product right away. There is no waiting for a reply after raising a request to an overseas headquarters. We want to deliver technology and products born in Japan to customers around the world at this same speed. We are waiting for people who will build that with us. Careers Delivering Japan-born AI products to customers around the world. The work of building the system to do that has only just begun. If you are interested in Sakana AI’s GTM team, please visit our careers page . 日本発のAIプロダクトを世界に売る：Sakana AI GTM責任者インタビュー Sakana AIは2026年、Sakana Chat、Sakana Marlin、Sakana Fugu、Sakana Translateなど、プロダクトを相次いでリリースしました。研究開発企業として知られてきたSakana AIは、研究から生まれたプロダクトを企業や官公庁に届ける段階に入っています。その販売と拡大を担うGTM（Go-To-Market）チームが、2026年9月に本格的に立ち上がりました。 チームを率いるのは、クラウド、IoT、ドローンといった新しい技術が新たな産業を形成する、その黎明期から事業の立ち上げを牽引してきた柿島さんです。なぜ今、Sakana AIなのか。研究から生まれたプロダクトをどう売り、どんなチームで広げていくのか。そして、まだ仕組みのないこのチームに今入る面白さはどこにあるのかについて聞きました。 インタビューイー 柿島 英和 Hidekazu Kakishima VP of GTM AWSの日本法人立ち上げ期に戦略的アカウントチームを率い、その後IoT通信スタートアップSORACOMの創業メンバー、米国ドローンメーカーSkydioでフライングロボティクスの社会実装を推進。現在はSakana AIにおいてプロダクト群の市場展開と価値提供に責任を持つ。 技術の最先端には新しいもの好きの優秀な人が集まる ── AWS、SORACOM、Skydio、そしてSakana AIと、新しい技術の立ち上げ期を選んでこられたように見えます。これまでのキャリアについて教えてください。 根っこにあるのは、テクノロジーは世界を良くしていくという思いです。そのため、新しい技術が生まれる領域の最先端で働きたいとずっと考えてきました。20代の頃はそこまで意識していなかったのですが、AWSというクラウドコンピューティングの技術に出会ってから、はっきりとそのモードに入ったと思います。 その後はSORACOMでIoT、Skydioでドローンに取り組み、今はAIです。いずれも新しい産業が生まれる領域で、その中にいる立場から先端の技術を市場に実装していく。それが私のやりたいことで、キャリアはずっとその基準で選んできました。 新しい領域の立ち上げ期を選び続けてきたのには、もう1つ理由があります。新しいトレンドが生まれると、その先端には新しいもの好きの優秀な人たちが集まるからです。最新の技術を学び、実装してお客さまに喜んでいただくこと自体ももちろん楽しいのですが、そうした人たちと一緒に働けることが、立ち上げ期ならではの面白さだと思っています。 ── そのうえで、なぜSakana AIだったのでしょうか。 日本で一番のAI企業だと思ったからです。スタートアップとして速く成長し、企業価値も急速に高まっている。そして、日本発でグローバルを目指し、研究開発を土台に持っている会社です。以前から注目はしていたのですが、知人に紹介してもらい、実際に話を聞く機会を得ました。 入社前に話したのは、共同創業者で社長の伊藤錬です。Sakana AIをスケールするビジネスとして、日本だけではなくグローバルで成長させていくというビジョンを聞いて、非常にワクワクしました。創業者もメンバーも素晴らしい人ばかりで、「いい人と一緒に働きたい」という気持ちが最後の決め手になりました。 研究開発から始まった会社なので、優れた技術があり、優秀な人が集まっています。ただ、それを世界で使えるものにしていくのは、決して簡単なことではありません。そこに向けてチームを作り、急拡大している最中だと感じましたし、その「使えるものにしていく」部分を、今まさにGTMチームが担っています。 研究で培った知見を、プロダクトとして幅広く届ける ── 「使えるものにしていく」というミッションについて伺います。GTMチームは今、どのような状況なのでしょうか。 Sakana AIは研究開発に加えて、金融や防衛といった業界に焦点を当てて、お客さまの現場にAIを実装してきました。そこで蓄積した知見をプロダクトという形にして、より幅広いお客さまに届けていくフェーズに入っています。 ただ、プロダクトを出せばすぐに使っていただけるかというと、そう簡単ではありません。プロダクトだけではお客さまの要件に応えきれない場面がどうしても出てきます。その間のギャップを埋めるために、今はFDE（Forward Deployed Engineer）の採用を進めているところです。 FDEがお客さまの現場で得た知見をプロダクトにフィードバックしていきます。それを積み重ねていくことで、将来的にはFDEが入らなくてもプロダクト単体で使っていただけるものを増やしていきたいと考えています。 FDEは多くのAI企業が力を入れている職種です。一方で、「お客さま先に入って開発するエンジニアと何が違うのか」と聞かれることもあります。そういったエンジニアとFDEとの違いは、まさにこのフィードバックの部分にあります。お客さまの課題を解決して終わりではなく、その経験をプロダクトの改善に反映するところまでがSakana AIのFDEの役割であり、目指す姿です。 トリガーはプロダクトだが解くのはお客さまの課題 ── GTMチームの募集ポジションの説明には「プロダクトドリブンなGTM」という言葉があります。SIerによる開発とも、SaaSプロダクトをそのまま導入するのとも違うように感じますが、どのようなアプローチなのでしょうか。 「プロダクトドリブン」というと、製品ありきで一方的に売り込む姿を想像される方も多いと思います。しかし、私たちのスタンスは少し違います。私たちが考えるプロダクトドリブンとは、プロダクトをお客さまとの対話のきっかけにするということです。まずプロダクトを提示して、お客さまの反応を見ながら、その解決策として最適な活用法をご提案していく。プロダクトを売りに行くというより、お客さまの課題にプロダクトを当てていく感覚に近いですね。 また、どう実装すればいいか分からない場面や、セキュリティを個別の要件に合わせる必要がある場面もあります。こうした要件は業界ごと、会社ごとに違うので、そこにFDEが入って導入を進めていきます。 一方で、個別の要件がなければ、プロダクトをそのまま使っていただけます。例えばAPIのサービスは、お客さまのシステムから直接呼び出して使う形です。Sakana Marlinはビジネス層向けの調査プロダクトで、日々調査業務にあたっている方々を主なターゲットにしています。 ── 自社のチームだけで売るわけではなく、パートナーとの協業も重視されていると伺いました。 私たちのリソースは限られていますから、パートナーの力は欠かせません。1つはSIerで、SIerにはSakana AIのプロダクトを各社のソリューションに組み込んでもらうよう働きかけています。もう1つはパートナーエコシステムを持つテクノロジー企業です。そのような企業のマーケットプレイスの中で、Sakana AIのプロダクトを提供してもらう形です。 この形であれば、日本だけではなくグローバルで使っていただけるユーザーを増やしていけます。 複数のモデルを協調させる「オーケストレーション」と、AI主権への手応え ── プロダクトの話をもう少し伺います。複数のフロンティアモデルを取り込む「オーケストレーション」は、Sakana AIが強みとする技術のひとつだと思います。お客さまの反応はいかがですか。 いろいろなモデルを使い分けられるようにする機能は、最近多くの会社が出しています。ただ、Sakana Fuguは単にモデルを切り替えるのではなく、複数のフロンティアモデルを協調させて1つのタスクにあたらせるというアプローチをとっています。これは非常にユニークな特徴だと思っています。 このアプローチが求められる背景には、どれほど優れたモデルであっても、単一のモデルに依存し続けることへの警戒があります。2026年2月には、米国政府が連邦機関にAnthropic製品の使用停止を指示し、米国防総省が同社をサプライチェーンリスクに指定する出来事がありました。どんなに性能が高くても、政治や契約の事情で使えなくなることがある。そのことを多くの企業が実感したはずです。 複数のモデルを使い分けたいという企業が増えてきていて、このアプローチに注目が集まっています。特定のモデルが突然使えなくなるのではないか、という不安も耳にします。こうした事情が良くも悪くも追い風になっていて、多くのお客さまから引き合いをいただいています。 ── AI主権という文脈でも、お客さまの反応は変わってきていますか。 変わってきていると感じます。AIはこれまでにないほど大きなトレンドで、それだけにセキュリティへの意識が非常に高まっています。「AI主権」「データ主権」への意識も、お客さま自身と政府の双方で上がってきていて、そうした要望は明らかに増えています。 しかも、気にされているのは大企業に限りません。中小企業の方々もデータ主権の観点で関心を持たれています。幅広いお客さまに共通するテーマになってきました。 ── 需要は多い一方で、お客さまも売る側もまだ手探りの状態だと感じます。これまで携わってきたクラウドやIoTという技術と比べて、何が同じで何が違うのでしょうか。 まず、AIは市場が圧倒的に大きい。そのうえで、お客さまの状態が違います。クラウドはオンプレミスからの置き換えという分かりやすい構図がありましたし、IoTも以前からM2M通信というものがあったのでお客さまの理解が早く、効率が上がるなら移行する、という判断が多かったのです。 AIはそうではなく、お客さま自身が手探りです。何をやればいいか分からない。しかも世界中の情報がインターネットでフラットに届くようになっているので、AIプレイヤーもお客さまも同時に悩んでいる状態です。そのため、営業としての難易度は上がっています。 ただ、お客さまは「何かやらないといけない」という強い危機感を持っています。やり方が分からないところに私たちがアプローチできるので、ビジネスはすごい勢いで動いています。一方で、モデルの進化が速すぎて、お客さまは長期のコミットを避ける傾向にあり、加えて、安心・安全に利用できる環境を求めています。 ── そうした市場の中で、1年後、3年後にどこを目指しているのでしょうか。 直近の優先順位は日本のお客さまで効果的な導入実績を増やしていくことです。ただ、グローバルでビジネスを展開していくにあたり、日本である程度の実績ができてから海外に持っていこうとしても、それでは遅い。ですから、最初から日本と海外を並行して進めるつもりで動いています。 日本では出資いただいている投資家の方々との連携や、さまざまなパートナーとの協業を通じて幅広く展開していきます。海外も同じ考え方で、出資いただいている海外のビッグテックなどと実績を作り、そこからスケールさせていく。3年後には、海外の比重のほうが大きくなっているのが理想です。 求めるのはドラスティックに動く環境を楽しめる人 ── ここからはチームの話を伺います。GTMチームでは、Account Executive、FDE、パートナーアライアンス、カスタマーサクセスと、複数の職種を募集します。職種ごとに、どのような人に来てほしいでしょうか。 まず、全職種に共通して言えることからお話しします。1つは、変化を楽しめることです。今は業界も社内も非常にドラスティックに動いていますので、それを楽しんで活躍できる人に来てほしいと思っています。そしてもう1つは好奇心です。お客さま、業界、社内のメンバーなど、幅広い人たちと関わりながら仕事を組み立てていくには好奇心が欠かせません。 そのうえで、Account Executiveについては、市場が大きく、私たちが販売する金額もダイナミックに増えていくと予想しています。大きなビジネスをゼロから組み立ててきた人、大型の案件をクローズしてきた人が望ましいです。パートナーアライアンスは、先ほどお話ししたSIerやエコシステムとの協業を担う役割で、誰と組み、どう一緒に売るかをゼロから設計していく仕事になります。 ── FDEについては、どのような人を求めていますか。 FDEには、お客さまの要望に対して「できません」から入らないでほしいと思っています。技術的な観点で、お客さまの要件と私たちのケイパビリティを照らし合わせたときに、そのギャップを埋める役割です。課題の発掘から解決まで、技術面でやり切れる人が向いています。 さらに言えば、スコープ外のところでも幅広く次の課題を見つけ、機会を探せる人に来てほしい。解決して終わりにせず、次に何が必要かを見つけて、プロダクトの改善につなげていく。それがSakana AIのFDEです。 ── 新たに募集するカスタマーサクセスは、導入後のお客さまを担当する役割ですね。 はい、導入していただいた後のフォローアップを担います。モデルの進化は速いので、きちんとした使い方ができているか、新たな課題が出ていないかを継続的に見ていく必要があります。これからプロダクトを積極的に出していきますから、それらを組み合わせてより効率的な仕組みにしていくのも、カスタマーサクセスの仕事です。 Account Executiveは役割上、次のお客さまへ向かっていきます。一方で、導入したお客さまをそのままにしておくと、他社に移ってしまったり、そもそもどうしていいか分からなくなったりする。そこを支える役割は、とても重要だと考えています。 2026年10月 Datadogのイベントにて登壇 仕組みを一緒に作っていけるのは今だけ ── 今、GTMチームに入るからこそ得られるものは何でしょうか。 まだ仕組み化できていないところがたくさんあるため、その仕組みを一緒に作っていけること。それが一番だと思います。 いろいろなバックグラウンドのメンバーが入ってきていて、それぞれの考え方や意見を持ち寄ってディスカッションしています。そこから新たな気づきがあったり、「新しいものを作るとはこういうことなのか」と実感できたりする。こういう経験ができる機会は、なかなかありません。AIという大きな波の中にいる会社で、ゼロから作っていく。これは貴重な経験だと思います。 そして、日本から世界へ。これはSakana AIだからこそできる挑戦です。Sakana AIは、開発の拠点が東京にあります。研究者も、プロダクトの開発チームも、GTMチームのすぐ隣のデスクに座っています。お客さまから得たフィードバックや機能追加の要望を、その場で開発側とディスカッションして、すぐにプロダクトに反映できる。海外の本社に要望を上げて返事を待つという時間は必要ありません。 日本で生まれた技術とプロダクトを、このスピード感のまま世界のお客さまに届けていく。それを一緒に作っていける方をお待ちしています。 採用情報 日本発のAIプロダクトを、世界のお客さまに届ける。その仕組みを作る仕事は、まだ始まったばかりです。Sakana AIのGTMチームに関心をお持ちの方は、ぜひ 採用情報ページ をご覧ください。
